newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Remote Aleutian island a paradise for birders.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Remote Aleutian island a paradise for birders.

text.p: To Second World War veterans who endured the bloody Battle of Attu -- and to U.S. Coast Guard crew members still stationed here -- the last island in Alaska's Aleutian chain, once likened by a national magazine to a prison colony, is known as a hardship post.

But to avid birdwatchers who migrate here each summer, treeless, rain-soaked Attu is paradise. They pay an Illinois-based tour company $5,000 each to fly here, bunk in rustic, abandoned military barracks and ride around on clunky bicycles, often in driving rain, just to catch glimpses of exotic Asian species blown off-course by Pacific storms.

When the visiting birders spot an important find, like an olive-tree pipit, a common greenshank, a black-backed wagtail, a long-toed stint or a ruff, they call their comrades by radio to pedal over and share the view.

"It's kind of the ultimate in birding in North America," said John Fritz, a retired firefighter from Long Island, New York. Non-birders cannot understand the attraction, he conceded. "They say, 'You're going all that way just to look at birds? You can look at birds here,'" he said, straddling his tour-issued bicycle and rolling his eyes.
"Hunters never have to explain. Gamblers never have to explain. But if you're a birder, you have to explain," said Jerry Rosenband of Glencoe, Illinois, who first came to Attu to watch birds in 1979.
"It's just wonderful to ride around on mountain bikes watching birds all day," said Californian Liz Hutson, who also spotted a spectacled eider, a threatened species.
MASS MIGRATION TO ALEUTIANS

Millions of seabirds migrate to the Aleutians to breed each summer, taking advantage of extended Alaskan summer daylight, plentiful fish and the absence of natural predators. But Attu is special for its proximity to Asia.

About 1,700 miles (2,700 km) west of Anchorage, Attu is so distant it is beyond the international dateline. It is so remote that a few of the exotic birds swept there by storms get separated permanently from their mates and wind up dying alone on the island. The birders welcome the ocean storms that blow the Asian birds off-course and say most of the strays make it back home safely.
"They're not really hopelessly lost," said birder Craig Roberts of Oregon.

Used to all kinds of bad weather, birders are unfazed by anything thrown at them on Attu, including summer snowflakes. And they are accustomed to rough conditions. "Birding is a contact sport -- contact with the ground," Rosenband said.

Ruggedly mountainous, dotted with lakes and crossed by clear streams, Attu is part of the sprawling Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Only 20 people -- crew members at a U.S. Coast Guard navigational station -- live on the island. The other resident is their shaggy and elderly dog, Coco.

But the remote island gets occasional visitors in addition to the birders and the sea otters frolicking offshore. Survivors of a bitter 1943 battle and their descendants sometimes make the long journey here. Attu, a federally protected historic battlefield, still shows scars left by the competing armies and is strewn with the rusted relics of war.
FINAL, BLOODY BATTLE IN 1943

U.S. forces retook the island from its Japanese occupiers 54 years ago. All but 29 of the more than 2,400 Japanese soldiers on the island died in the 1943 battle, hundreds of them at their own hands when U.S. victory was imminent. U.S. casualties totalled 549 deaths and 1,148 wounded.
On the top of Engineer Hill, site of the Japanese soldiers' desperate last stand, the Japanese government in 1987 erected a star-shaped monument.
Birdwatchers are well aware of the wartime history, and they and the visiting veterans sometimes mingle.
"When I first came here in 1989 it was just haunted," said Jerry Swertinski, an operating nurse from Delaware who was making his sixth birding trip to Attu.
But for people who are not bird watchers, Second World War buffs or experts in the culture of Alaska's Aleut people, the island is an obscurity.

Second World War pilot John Geddes, who returned in June to the bay where enemy fire shot him down -- "It was the best landing I ever swam away from," he said, standing on the beach 55 years later -- believes Attu willy always be a mere historical footnote. "One guy told me, 'The only people who know what Attu is are crossword-puzzle addicts,'" Geddes said.
